name: PT Mandiri Herindo Adiperkasa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Mandiri Herindo Adiperkasa - a coal hauler priced for a contract loss the book does not show
frontmatter.summary: Mandiri Herindo Adiperkasa hauls coal from mine stockpiles to jetties in Kalimantan, paid a rupiah tariff per tonne on a contract book that runs to 2034. The data pack understates its depreciation, and therefore its EBITDA and cash flow, because the fleet is leased. At a low single-digit multiple of enterprise value to restated EBITDA the equity is priced for the end of the coal cycle; we initiate at BUY.
thesis: A hauling contractor, not a miner: the company moves other operators' coal from ROM stockpile to jetty on a per-tonne tariff, owns no reserve and pays no royalty, so the lens is tonnes, tariff, fleet utilisation and the lease book, never a reserve NAV [S2, S6].

The data pack carries only the G&A depreciation line, so its D&A, EBITDA and cash flow are materially understated: the filings show total D&A of IDR369.2bn in FY2025 and total capital expenditure, including leased fleet, of IDR605.0bn, giving EBITDA of IDR852.4bn on revenue of IDR2,922.3bn [S2].

The contract book is long and concentrated: PT Indonesia Pratama (Bayan) supplied IDR1,863.3bn of FY2025 revenue on a contract that runs to 2034, the related party PT Mandiri Intiperkasa IDR307.5bn, and the new Ade Putra Tanrajeng contract adds IDR2,200.0bn to 2030; the trade-off is that one group is most of the book [S2, S4, S8].

At Rp132 the shares trade at 2.6x FY2025 restated EBITDA on the FY2025 year-end net financial liabilities of IDR46.2bn — the 30 June bridge date carries more lease debt, so the same arithmetic gives a slightly higher multiple there — and 8.9x earnings, with a trailing dividend yield of 9.1%; the market value is IDR2,164.1bn before deducting the listed coal stake worth IDR264.6bn [S0, S4].

Our DCF at the desk's through-cycle deck, with the hauling spread calibrated to the FY2025 actual, gives Rp225; the base-case target is Rp241 and the probability-weighted target Rp244, 94.1% including the dividend. The bear case at Rp115 sits below the price, so the BUY rests on the base and bull branches rather than on a floor [S2, S4].

catalysts.event: Fourth-quarter 2026 run-rate and the first full quarter under the Ade Putra contract
FY2026 audited results and the AGM dividend decision; the board has paid a dividend in each year since listing
Kideco Jaya Agung and related-party Mandiri Intiperkasa hauling contracts expire and are re-tendered
Ade Putra Tanrajeng hauling contract ends; the Bayan book runs to 2034

blocks.text: **Rating: BUY · target Rp244 · last close Rp132 · return 94.1%**

Mandiri Herindo Adiperkasa moves coal. It does not mine it: the company runs prime movers with double trailers, single trailers and dump trucks between a customer's ROM stockpile or crusher and its jetty, loading point or port stockpile, and is paid a rupiah tariff per tonne hauled, with the tariff reset periodically against fuel and labour [S2, S6]. In FY2025 it hauled 60.3 million tonnes, a 7.2% share of national coal output of 834.1 million tonnes, on revenue of IDR2,922.3bn [S2, S3, S6]. The business is a fleet, a contract book and a lease obligation; there is no reserve to value and no royalty to pay, which is why the industry's DCF-on-cash-flow method, not a mine NAV, is the right frame [S2].

The first thing a reader should understand is that the data pack is wrong in a specific, mechanical way. The filings carry total depreciation and amortisation of IDR369.2bn on revenue of IDR2,922.3bn, against a pack line of a few billion rupiah that captures only the G&A depreciation. The fleet is largely leased on three-year terms, so most of the charge is right-of-use amortisation rather than owner depreciation, and most of the fleet investment is non-cash lease additions rather than the cash-capex line [S2, S4]. We restate D&A, capital expenditure and operating profit for the four years the data history covers, rebuild EBITDA at IDR852.4bn and charge the full fleet investment in the forecast. None of the restatements changes a cash flow; they change where the reader sees it.

The variant view is not that coal prices rise. It is that the market has priced this company as if the coal-hauling book were about to end, while the book is contracted to 2034 with its largest customer, to 2031 with Darma Henwa, to 2030 with a new customer signed in October 2026, and to 2027 with the two contracts now up for renewal [S2, S4]. At Rp132 the shares are worth IDR2,164.1bn; against FY2025 net financial liabilities of IDR46.2bn and before deducting the IDR264.6bn listed stake, the enterprise is priced at 2.6x FY2025 EBITDA [S0, S4]. Our DCF, at a nominal cost of capital for a rupiah cash flow, gives Rp225 a share; the base-case target is Rp241 and the probability-weighted target Rp244 [S2, S4].

What moves the value, in order. First, the hauling spread: fuel is 29.9% of cost of revenue and the tariff recovers it with a lag, which is exactly what compressed the nine-month 2026 gross margin from 20.1% in FY2025 toward the FY2026E level of 16.0% [S2, S4]. Second, the contract book: renewal of the Kideco and Mandiri Intiperkasa contracts at the end of 2027, and the ramp of the Ade Putra contract signed in October 2026 [S2, S4, S8]. Third, capital allocation: the company has been the buyer of a stake in a listed coal producer that its own public expose ties to one of its customer groups, marked through profit and loss, and a 10.0% liquidity discount applies to the target because traded value is below the house floor [S0, S3, S4].

Coal hauling in Indonesia sits between the mine and the barge. Most producers contract the road and stockpile movement to specialist fleets rather than run it themselves, because the capital intensity, the maintenance burden and the safety record required by the mine's ESG covenants are different from the mining business. The contractors that survive are those with long-term contracts, a fleet that can be financed, and a record that survives the buyer's audits. The business is cyclical through the volumes the mines choose to move and through the diesel price, not through the coal price itself.

The company was founded in 1994 as a mining-products transporter, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in July 2023 and operates from Jakarta through the Mandiri Services brand [S0, S3]. Its revenue comes from coal transportation services, with a small mineral-transport and road-maintenance component: the FY2025 segment note puts IDR2,535.6bn of third-party revenue in East Kalimantan and IDR307.5bn in North Kalimantan, the latter the related-party customer, with a small balance in Central Kalimantan, and the annual report describes coal hauling, coal loading and road maintenance as the service lines [S2, S6]. The hauling is mostly long-distance road movement with large payloads: the fleet at the end of 2024 comprised 208 prime movers with double trailers in the largest payload class, 157 dump trucks and a smaller number of single-trailer units, spread over six work locations and seven coal transportation projects in three provinces [S6].

The customer list is the asset, and it is short. PT Indonesia Pratama, which the company's public expose labels with the BYAN ticker, supplied IDR1,863.3bn of FY2025 revenue; related party PT Mandiri Intiperkasa supplied IDR307.5bn; Darma Henwa and Kideco Jaya Agung supplied the large majority of the rest, and the four customers disclosed as exceeding a tenth of revenue together account for almost the whole top line [S2, S3]. That is a concentration a lender would underwrite and an equity investor must discount, and the contracts are correspondingly long: the Indonesia Pratama agreement runs to the end of 2034, Darma Henwa to April 2031, Mandiri Intiperkasa and Kideco to the end of 2027, and the new PT Ade Putra Tanrajeng agreement signed on 6 October 2026 to the end of 2030 [S2, S4].

The operating model is deliberately capital-light on the balance sheet and heavy on the lease book. The company owns land, buildings and part of the heavy equipment outright, but it acquires much of the fleet through right-of-use leases from finance companies, with three-year terms and implicit interest rates in the high single digits to ten per cent [S4]. At the end of September 2026 right-of-use assets were still the larger half of the operating asset base, and lease liabilities were most of the debt stack [S4]. The company does not hedge the coal price, because it does not sell coal; it buys diesel, tyres, spare parts and labour and sells tonnes moved, and its contract tariffs are its hedge.

Strategy as the company frames it is to deepen the contract book with existing customers, add third-party volumes as producing groups consolidate their hauling into fewer contractors, and hold cost down through component fabrication and maintenance discipline [S6]. The evidence of the last four years is a fleet build: total capital expenditure, including leased fleet, was IDR187.3bn in FY2022, IDR776.6bn in FY2023, IDR498.7bn in FY2024 and IDR605.0bn in FY2025, against EBITDA that rose from IDR562.0bn to IDR852.4bn [S2, S9]. That build is finished for now: in the nine months to September 2026 the company added only IDR19.7bn of new right-of-use assets [S4]. The mix shift toward longer-haul work, with the Bayan contract the largest single piece of the book, is the most likely reason revenue has grown faster than tonnes [S2, S3].

Control sits with PT Edika Agung Mandiri, which holds just over a third of the shares, and with members of the Sugianto family and the founding management, who together hold the large majority of the register; the free float is 20.4% [S2, S0]. The company employs 2,457 people and is a challenger rather than the scale leader in a fragmented hauling market, with the market position resting on a handful of relationships rather than on a resource or a network [S0, S6]. Section six deals with what the ownership structure means for minority holders.

The industry this company sells into is the road and stockpile movement of Indonesian thermal coal. National output was 834.1 million tonnes in 2024, the year the company reported a 7.2% share of it, and the hauling market is the layer between the mine gate and the barge or vessel [S6]. Demand for hauling is therefore a function of mine output and of hauling distance, not of the coal price directly; but the coal price determines whether a marginal mine produces, how far it can afford to move coal, and how much the producer is willing to pay a contractor, so the cycle still reaches the hauler through volume and tariff [S2].

Our house coal deck, the desk's forecast series rather than a company disclosure, has Newcastle 6,000 kcal NAR at 137.0 US$/t in FY2026E, 118.0 in FY2027E and 150.3 at the spot print, against a long-run anchor of 105.0, with the through-cycle level set against marginal Indonesian supply cost. Our house oil deck has Brent at 96.0 in FY2026E against a FY2025 average of 68.1, easing to 75.0 long run. For MAHA the oil path is the live one: fuel is 29.9% of cost of revenue, bought chiefly from Pertamina, and the tariff recovers it with a lag, so a Brent spike compresses the gross margin for as long as the reset takes [S2, S4]. The coal deck is not a mechanical input in this model: the template's coal cost link is zero because there is no coal purchase in cost of revenue, and we do not tie the revenue path to the Newcastle series; coal prices reach the hauler only indirectly through the volumes the mines choose to move and the tariffs they can bear, which we model from the contract book [S2, S6].

Regulation reaches the company in three ways. Mining licences and annual work plans determine which customers produce and how much; the domestic market obligation and the price cap determine the economics of the domestic coal the hauler moves; and export-proceeds retention and the coal royalty regime change the relative attraction of domestic versus export volumes for the producers, which changes the demand for hauling to a domestic jetty against hauling to an export stockpile [S2, S6]. None of these is a licence the company holds — it is a service provider to the licence holders — so its regulatory risk is second-hand but real.

Competition is fragmented and local. Hauling is a relationship business in which the buyer cares about fleet availability, safety record and cost per tonne-kilometre; barriers are contracts, working capital and the ability to finance a fleet, not geology or a permit [S6]. The company's position is a mid-sized specialist with long-standing contracts at Kideco, Bayan, Mandiri Intiperkasa and Darma Henwa; its moat is the multi-year contract and the demonstrated safety and execution record that wins the buyer's audit, and its weakness is that the buyer has market power once the contract is up for renewal [S2, S6].

The five forces are clear. Buyer power is high: a handful of mine operators award the contracts, and the largest is most of the book [S2]. Supplier power is moderate: fuel is a commodity supplied by a state company and tyres and parts are competitive, but the finance companies that lease the fleet are concentrated and set the cost of capital [S4]. New entrants are a constant threat at the low end, because a competitor can bid a fleet into a contract, but the safety and scale requirements at the large mines limit the credible list. Substitutes are the energy transition and the shift of coal logistics toward conveyor and rail, a slow erosion rather than a step change within our horizon. Rivalry is on price and fleet availability, and returns depend on contract discipline and on keeping the fleet utilised, which is exactly what the financials show [S2, S6].

Revenue grew from IDR1,641.9bn in FY2022 to IDR2,922.3bn in FY2025, with tonnes rising from 60.0 million to 60.3 million over FY2024 and FY2025 and the rest of the growth coming from mix and the tariff [S2, S3]. The FY2025 increase of 14.9% on essentially flat tonnage is the tariff and the contract mix, not volume [S2, S3]. The five-year shape in the table matches the company's own five-year highlight, which shows revenue rising through the same years on the same basis [S3].

The cost structure is a fleet cost structure. Fuel of IDR697.7bn, repair and maintenance, salaries, right-of-use amortisation of IDR201.1bn and fixed-asset depreciation are the five large lines of the FY2025 cost of revenue, and together they are almost all of it [S2]. That is why the gross margin moves with diesel and with utilisation, and why the company's operating leverage is high: a tariff that lags fuel by a quarter can take several points of the gross margin away, as it did in the nine months to September 2026 [S4].

The restatement matters here. The data pack shows D&A of a few billion rupiah and the rebuilt series shows IDR702.4bn of EBITDA in FY2024 and IDR852.4bn in FY2025, against pack figures that understate both because they capture only the G&A depreciation charge [S0, S2]. The filings' segment note reports total D&A of IDR280.9bn in FY2024 and IDR369.2bn in FY2025, and total capital expenditure including leased fleet of IDR498.7bn and IDR605.0bn [S2]. On the restated numbers the EBITDA margin was 27.6% in FY2024 and 29.2% in FY2025, and ROE was 12.9% [S2].

The FY2025 headline profit is the one number that looks worse than the business. Operating profit rose to IDR483.2bn from IDR421.4bn, but net profit fell to IDR242.5bn from IDR296.7bn because of a non-cash unrealised loss of IDR118.5bn on the 2.1% stake in PT Prima Andalan Mandiri Tbk, a listed coal producer that the company's own public expose labels with the ticker of one of its customer groups [S2, S3, S4]. The stake cost IDR235.6bn and was carried at IDR264.6bn at the end of September 2026, so the cumulative mark is positive; the FY2025 loss was the reversal of a prior gain, not cash leaving the company [S4]. We take the stake out of the operating forecast and value it at market in the bridge, and we set other non-operating income to zero rather than forecast a mark-to-market that moves with someone else's share price [S4].

The nine months to September 2026 show the cycle position. Revenue of IDR2,331.0bn was up on the prior-year period, but gross profit of IDR360.7bn was only slightly higher, a margin just above fifteen per cent against 20.1% for FY2025, and operating profit of IDR253.5bn was below the prior-year period [S4]. Net profit of IDR167.9bn was more than double because the mark-to-market loss was much smaller than a year earlier [S4]. The forecast reproduces that: we hold the base-input gross margin at the FY2025 full-year actual of 20.2% and let the deck's Brent path, at 58.0% pass-through, compress it to 16.0% in FY2026E and release it toward 18.9% by FY2030E as Brent normalises [S2, S4].

The fuel link deserves its own paragraph because FY2025 looks like a contradiction. Fuel cost rose to IDR697.7bn from IDR514.7bn while the deck's Brent fell from 79.8 to 68.1, and tonnage was flat [S2, S6]. Revenue per tonne rose on the same tonnage, which means longer hauls and more litres per tonne; the last disclosed fuel volume, for FY2024, is 57.0 thousand kilolitres, and at that consumption the FY2025 cost implies a higher price per litre than FY2024 [S6]. The residual is Pertamina's administered diesel price, which does not track Brent one-for-one. In 9M2026 fuel cost rose to IDR686.5bn from IDR468.6bn while Brent was at 96.0, so the link reasserted itself; the nine-month margin of just above fifteen per cent against the FY2025 full-year base of 20.2% implies that about 58.0% of the fuel move passed through, which is the coefficient we use [S2, S4]. We calibrate against the FY2025 full-year margin rather than the nine-month 2025 comparative (gross profit IDR350.7bn on revenue IDR2,024.5bn), because FY2025 fuel rose while the tariff reset caught up only in the fourth quarter, so the 2025 nine-month period already carries part of the same compression [S2, S4]. At zero pass-through the DCF is still above the share price, and at full pass-through it is materially higher, so the conclusion does not depend on this coefficient.

Revenue is modelled from the last actual forward. Nine-month revenue annualises to a run-rate above FY2025, and FY2026E grows 8.0% to IDR3,156.1bn; the nine months already show Indonesia Pratama revenue at IDR1,470.5bn against IDR1,235.6bn and Kideco at IDR220.2bn against IDR184.2bn, so the customer book was still growing before the new contract started [S4]. FY2026E carries one ramp quarter of the Ade Putra contract; FY2027E grows 13.3% to IDR3,575.9bn on a full year of it, worth IDR2,200.0bn over four years and about IDR550.0bn a year, roughly a sixth of revenue [S4, S8]. Net profit is IDR248.3bn in FY2026E, held down by the fuel squeeze, and recovers to IDR347.2bn in FY2027E as the spread normalises and the new contract contributes [S2, S4].

Cash conversion is the reason the equity is interesting. Operating cash flow was positive in FY2025, and the gap to EBITDA is the lease service and the working-capital build [S2, S4]. Total capital expenditure, including leased fleet, peaked at IDR776.6bn in FY2023 and IDR605.0bn in FY2025, and the nine months to September 2026 added only IDR19.7bn of new right-of-use assets [S4, S9]. That is the harvest phase: FCFF jumps from IDR100.7bn in FY2025 to IDR376.1bn in FY2026E and holds at IDR399.4bn in FY2027E on our definition, which charges capex including right-of-use additions [S2, S4]. The pause is deployment timing, not the end of the fleet cycle: the leases are three-year terms and IDR287.6bn of minimum lease payments fall due within one year, with a further IDR233.2bn over the remainder of the lease book, so replacement starts from FY2027E. Our capex path rises from 5.5% of revenue in FY2026E to 14.5% by FY2030E, restoring the full D&A-plus-growth charge by FY2028 rather than deferring it [S4 note 11].

Working capital is the soft spot. Trade receivables rose and trade payables fell in the nine months to September 2026, taking operating working capital to about eleven to twelve per cent of annualised revenue against a year-end norm of four to five per cent in each of the last two Decembers, and the related-party trade receivable from PT Mandiri Intiperkasa rose [S0, S2, S4]. The payable contraction is not only seasonal: cash paid to suppliers rose faster than revenue against the prior-year nine months, and payable days fell from about sixty-one at the December year-end to about thirty-three at September [S4]. We therefore hold working capital at 8.0% of revenue, between the year-end history and the September level, and we flag the related-party balance as a governance item rather than an accounting error [S2, S4]. Holding the September ratio instead would lower FY2026E free cash flow by the one-off increase in the working-capital balance and turn the net-cash build into a small net-debt position; that is the downside case in the risk table.

The balance sheet is leveraged on paper and liquid in practice. At the end of September 2026 cash was IDR459.1bn, lease liabilities were the bulk of the debt stack and the Bank Mandiri investment credit drawn in January 2026 to buy land was IDR43.3bn at a fixed rate [S4]. Net financial liabilities at the FY2025 year-end were IDR46.2bn, or 0.1x EBITDA; the September LK shows gross debt down, but cash also fell by more as the FY2025 dividend and the lease principal were paid, so net debt was higher at that date [S4]. The company pays a dividend of 12 rupiah a share — a payout of 81.1% of FY2025 parent profit — and has done so in each year since listing, within a policy that allows up to 40.0% of retained earnings after mandatory reserves [S2, S6].

The earnings-quality screens are mixed and the split matters. Accruals are clean: net profit and operating cash flow track each other once the non-cash mark is removed, and there is no persistent gap [S2]. The divergence flags fire on working capital and on the capitalised lease book: receivables outgrew revenue in the first half of 2026 before unwinding in the third quarter, and the related-party revenue line is a tenth of the top line [S0, S2, S4]. The structure flags are the concentrated controlling stake, the treasury buyback of a fraction of the shares, and the stake in a listed coal producer tied to one of the customer groups [S2, S4]. None of these is manipulation-class on the evidence; they are optics-class and we treat them as such, in the bear case and in section six.

We value MAHA primarily on a discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm, because the business is worth the tariff it earns on tonnes and the cash it converts, and because the alternatives are weaker for this name. A reserve NAV does not apply: there is no reserve. A multiple is a cross-check only, because the peer set is a mixed group of small-cap traders, barge operators, terminals and shippers whose prices and data-pack EBITDA are not comparable, and because the company's own 2023-25 multiples span the post-IPO cycle [S0]. We therefore weight the DCF at 90.0% and P/BV at 10.0%. We have removed the EV/EBITDA cross-check entirely: the peer median is struck on data-pack EBITDA measured before the lease and D&A restatement MAHA needs, so applying it to restated EBITDA would mix two definitions. The P/BV cross-check uses book equity, which is comparable, and we explain the divergence rather than average it away [S0, S2].

The cost of capital is a rupiah build. The risk-free rate of 7.4%, the Indonesian sovereign default spread of 1.6%, the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5% are the house cost-of-capital inputs carried in the desk configuration, not the company's filing; with a levered beta of 1.20, they give a cost of equity of 13.9%. Debt is 20.5% of the capital structure at a pre-tax cost of 9.4%, the blend of the lease implicit rates disclosed in the notes and the fixed-rate Bank Mandiri facility [S4], giving a weighted average cost of capital of 12.5%. Terminal growth is 3.2%, the peer median and essentially the deck's long-run Indonesian CPI, rather than the higher house rate used in the first draft.

The engine produces Rp225 a share from an enterprise value of IDR3,709.6bn, with the terminal value at 39.8% of the total. The cash flows that support it are the demonstrated ones: EBITDA of IDR852.4bn on the restated D&A, capex normalising after the fleet build, and a working-capital drag only in the near term [S2, S4]. The DCF is most sensitive to the hauling spread and to the cost of capital, as the sensitivity table shows.

The bridge deliberately pairs the 30 June 2026 cash and debt from the data pack so that the cash balance and the discounted H2 2026 cash flow cover the same period. Using the September cash with the June debt line would double-count the third quarter, which is already inside the September cash balance. On the September LK the company has less debt and less cash than in June; the forecast uses that statement, but the bridge stays on the June date. The model then builds net cash: cash reaches IDR563.5bn against IDR462.4bn of debt at FY2026E, and IDR640.7bn against IDR362.4bn at FY2027E, before the IDR264.6bn listed stake, which is a balance-sheet cushion the market does not pay for at today's price [S4]. The listed stake is carried at its 30 September 2026 market price and the P/BV check uses 30 September book equity, while the bridge's cash and debt are 30 June; the mismatch is one quarter's mark and is immaterial to the target. The thesis multiple of 2.6x uses FY2025 year-end net financial liabilities; on the 30 June bridge date, with higher lease debt, the same EBITDA gives a multiple a little above that figure, and neither version deducts the IDR264.6bn stake.

The surviving cross-check is the P/BV method, and the divergence is informative. At 1.8 times book it gives Rp200, -11.1% versus the DCF, because the peer median book multiple is barely above book while this company earned a double-digit return on equity in FY2025; it is a floor check, not a target [S0]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check would give a number several times the DCF because the peer median multiple is struck on data-pack EBITDA measured before the lease restatement; we do not print it as a method because a reader cannot compare it to the denominator we use, and it is excluded from the blend entirely. P/BV carries the remaining weight, and the DCF-driven value is Rp223.

What does today's price imply? We invert the model on revenue growth: at Rp132 the market is paying for FY2027E revenue growth of 3.7%, far below the contract-book path, with the spread held at our base level [S0]. Put differently, the enterprise value of the operating business is a low single-digit multiple of EBITDA, and the market gives almost no credit for the IDR264.6bn listed stake or for the net cash the model builds. Either the market knows a contract loss the filings do not show, or it is applying a governance and liquidity discount so large that it has become the whole valuation. We treat the discount explicitly: the target carries a 10.0% haircut because traded value is below the house floor, and the governance discount enters the bear case through a higher cost of capital [S0].

The output contract of our commodity-cyclical method, adapted to a service business. Through-cycle NAV is the DCF above, which prices diesel on the deck's full path — spiking in FY2026, normalising to the long-run anchor thereafter — rather than at the spot print; the spot Brent carry is a timing input and is not in the base case [S2]. There is no reserve life and no realisation haircut to apply — the tariff is contracted. The dividend anchor the coal sector normally relies on is present: trailing yield is 9.1% and the through-cycle dividend yield at our FY2027E payout is 13.0%, which is a floor on the equity's value for a shareholder who believes the contract book [S0]. Net debt to trough EBITDA is below one times on the restated numbers, so the equity survives a trough without dilution [S4]. The frame carries the macro tilt: thermal coal is neutral, the oil-import and rupiah-rate-sensitive names are avoided, and this name's exposure is to diesel and to mine volumes, not to the rupiah financing market.

The bear case is a contract, terminal-value and spread story, not a solvency story. It assumes the Kideco and Mandiri Intiperkasa contracts are re-tendered away at the end of 2027 rather than renewed — close to a fifth of revenue — that Indonesia Pratama/Bayan, the largest customer and most of the book, trims hauling volumes as its mine plan shifts, that the spread stays at the nine-month 2026 level because diesel runs ahead of the tariff reset, that the governance discount persists through a higher cost of capital, and that terminal growth falls to near zero as the energy transition reaches the customer mines. On those shocks our bear case gives Rp115, below the last close: the market is already pricing something close to the bear [S2, S4, S6].

The bull case is deliberately not a full mirror. Brent eases toward the through-cycle path and the spread recovers toward the FY2025 level, the Ade Putra contract ramps while the Kideco and Mandiri Intiperkasa contracts renew on schedule, the Bayan book holds, and the market closes part of the governance discount as the dividend record holds and the listed stake is re-rated. It gives Rp487. Both branches shock the same four levers — revenue growth, gross margin, the cost of capital and terminal growth — but the bull's revenue and margin shocks are three-quarters the size of the bear's, because the bear is a specific contract-loss and transition case while the bull only assumes the cycle normalises; a full mirror would require volume growth beyond the contract book with no source [S2, S4]. Terminal growth is not lifted in the bull: it stays at the base 3.2%, close to the deck's long-run CPI, because there is no source for perpetual real growth above CPI in a per-tonne hauling service, while the bear's cut to near zero is the sourced energy-transition case [S6]. The probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | What we watch | |---|---|---|---| | Customer concentration — the Bayan book is most of revenue | High | High | Contract renewals and any change in tonnes moved for Indonesia Pratama; a volume trim is the bear case [S2] | | Spread compression as diesel runs ahead of the tariff reset | High | Medium | Quarterly gross margin against the deck's Brent path [S2, S4] | | Contract renewal at Kideco and Mandiri Intiperkasa, both ending 2027 | Medium | High | Tender outcomes and the awarded tariff [S2] | | Related-party gravity — revenue and a receivable from PT Mandiri Intiperkasa, and the stake in a listed producer tied to that group | Medium | High | Related-party disclosures and any new affiliate transaction [S2, S4] | | Capital allocation — the listed stake marked through profit and loss | Medium | Medium | The investment-in-shares note and the mark direction each quarter [S4] | | Working capital — receivables outgrowing payables and suppliers tightening | Medium | Medium | Trade receivables and payables in each quarterly filing; a structural move to the top of the observed range would absorb several quarters of free cash flow [S4] | | Liquidity — thin free float and concentrated control | High | Medium | Free float, traded value and any exchange announcement [S0] | | Terminal value — most of the DCF sits beyond the forecast | Low within the horizon | High beyond it | Terminal growth is 3.2%, close to the deck's long-run CPI, and the bear case cuts it to near zero [S6] | | Energy transition — coal volumes and hauling distance over the horizon | Low within the horizon | High beyond it | National output and the customer mines' plans [S6] |

What would change our view: a lost Kideco or Mandiri Intiperkasa contract would say the book is shrinking rather than re-tendering; a sustained gross margin below the nine-month 2026 level would say the spread is structural rather than cyclical; a large new related-party transaction would say the governance discount is warranted; and a dividend cut or a rights issue would say the cash is not as accessible as the balance sheet suggests [S2, S4].

Ownership is concentrated and family-led. PT Edika Agung Mandiri holds just over a third of the shares, the Sugianto family and management hold most of the rest, and the free float is 20.4% [S2, S0]. The president director and a director are among the named shareholders, and the president commissioner is a shareholder too, which means the board is elected by the same group that runs the company [S2, S3]. The board has one independent commissioner out of three; on the disclosed composition that is a thin independent presence for a company of this size, and we treat it as a governance fact rather than a technicality [S3]. We found no evidence of a pledged controlling stake in the filings, and no rights issue since listing; the only equity action is a buyback that left a small treasury holding [S2].

Related-party gravity is the main governance issue, and it runs in three directions. The company earns a tenth of its revenue from PT Mandiri Intiperkasa, a customer disclosed as a related party and labelled with the MCOL ticker in the company's own public expose, and it has invested IDR235.6bn for 2.1% of the listed PT Prima Andalan Mandiri Tbk, carried at IDR264.6bn at the end of September 2026 [S2, S3, S4]. On the cost side it buys from related parties too: PT Mandala Karya Prima and PT Alat Bumi Permai supplied part of the FY2025 cost of revenue, and the heavy-vehicle leases include related-party lessors on three-year terms [S2, S4]. None of these is disclosed as being on other than normal commercial terms, and none is a transfer of cash out of the operating business on the evidence; but the combination of a related customer, related suppliers and an equity stake in the same group is exactly the structure on which this exchange has historically destroyed minority value, and it is why we do not value the stake above its listed price and why the discount in the bear case is real [S2, S4].

The audit history is conventional. The FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja with an unmodified opinion, and the balance sheet is on a going-concern basis [S2]. The dividend record is good for an IDX small cap: the company has paid a dividend in each year since listing, with dividends paid of IDR196.7bn in FY2025 within a policy of up to 40.0% of retained earnings after mandatory reserves [S2, S6]. The buyback and the stake purchase are the two capital-allocation decisions a minority holder should weigh: the buyback used corporate cash to acquire shares, and the stake used corporate cash to buy a listed coal producer at a mark that has moved through profit and loss [S4].

We could not verify the current IDX board or notation status from an exchange announcement in this window, and we make no claim beyond the filings. On ESG, the exposures are the usual ones for a coal hauler: the emissions of the coal it moves, the safety and labour conditions of its driver workforce, and the transition risk of its customer base. The annual report documents safety and community programmes, and the company has received zero-accident and mining-practice awards from its customers and the provincial government, but the filings do not quantify emissions or incident rates in a way we can use in the valuation [S6]. We treat ESG as a slow erosion of terminal value rather than an independent driver within our horizon.

The near catalyst has already passed: the nine-month 2026 accounts were filed in October 2026, and they show the margin squeeze and the working-capital build we have modelled [S4]. The next is the FY2026 audited result and the AGM early next year, where the board decides the dividend on FY2026E parent profit of IDR248.3bn, up from IDR242.5bn after the mark-to-market loss, against the much higher FY2024 base; a maintained rupiah-per-share dividend would be a statement that the cash is real [S2]. The new Ade Putra contract, signed on 6 October 2026 and running to the end of 2030, should start contributing from the fourth quarter of 2026 and is worth about IDR550.0bn a year at full run-rate [S4, S8].

The medium-term catalyst is the renewal cycle at the end of 2027, when the Kideco and Mandiri Intiperkasa contracts expire and are re-tendered [S2]. A clean renewal at a similar tariff would remove the main bear-case leg; a loss would validate it. The Bayan contract runs to 2034 and is the anchor of the book, so its terms — and any volume change from the mine — matter more than any other single disclosure [S2].

We monitor each quarter: tonnes hauled against the company's FY2026 target of 65.0 million tonnes; the gross margin against the deck's diesel path; the trade receivables and payables that determine whether the working-capital build reverses; the related-party balances and the mark on the MCOL stake; and the lease additions and principal repayments that tell us whether the fleet is in harvest or replacement mode [S4, S2]. We also watch traded value, because the target carries a liquidity discount and a thinner tape would widen it [S0].

bear.narrative: The coal-price bid fades faster than the tariff reset and the hauling spread stays at the nine-month 2026 level for longer. The Kideco and related-party Mandiri Intiperkasa contracts, both ending 31 December 2027, are re-tendered away rather than renewed; Indonesia Pratama/Bayan, 64% of the book, trims hauling volumes as its mine plan shifts, so the largest customer is no longer the anchor the base case assumes. The market's governance discount persists through a higher cost of capital and the terminal value is cut to a near-zero-growth hauling business as the energy transition reaches the customer mines.

bull.narrative: Brent eases back toward the through-cycle path and the hauling spread recovers toward the FY2025 level, the Ade Putra and Kideco contracts ramp on schedule, the Bayan book holds, and the market closes part of the governance discount as the dividend record and the MCOL stake are re-rated. The upside is taken in the explicit forecast years only: terminal growth is held at the base rate, the deck's long-run CPI, because there is no source for perpetual real growth above it in a per-tonne hauling service.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 revenue was Rp2,331.0bn, 15.1% above the same period of 2025, and annualising the run-rate gives Rp3,108.0bn before any contribution from the Ade Putra Tanrajeng contract signed 6 October 2026 (S4, S8). We set FY2026E at +8.0% to carry one ramp quarter of a contract worth about Rp550bn a year, and FY2027E at +13.3%: a full year of Ade Putra adds Rp550bn, while the rest of the book grows with the Bayan and Kideco momentum shown in 9M2026 (Indonesia Pratama revenue +19.0% and Kideco +19.6%, S4). Growth then fades to 5%, 4% and 3% as the contract book matures and settles at the 3.25% terminal rate. No volume haircut: the company's FY2026 target is 65.0 Mt against 60.31 Mt hauled in FY2025 (S3).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 20.15% (Rp588.8bn on Rp2,922.3bn, S2) at deck Brent of US$68.1, so that is the base-input-cost margin. FY2025 fuel cost rose 35.5% while Brent fell 14.7%, but tonnage was flat and revenue per tonne rose 14.4%, so a large part of the fuel-per-tonne rise is haul mix: the last disclosed litres (FY2024, 56,952 kL on 60.05 Mt, S6) put fuel cost at about Rp9,038/kL, and longer hauls raise litres per tonne. The residual is Pertamina's administered diesel price. In 9M2026 fuel cost rose 46.5% against Brent +41%, so the cost link reasserted itself; the 9M gross margin of 15.5% against 20.15% implies a within-year pass-through of about 58% of the fuel move (S4), which we use below. The base-input margin stays at the last actual; the compression comes back through the link as Brent normalises.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal is not a cost of the hauling contractor: the FY2025 cost of revenue has no coal purchase line, only fuel, repair and maintenance, salaries, leases and depreciation (S2 note 22). Set to zero; the coal price reaches the P&L through mine operators' volumes, captured in revenue growth.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: No coal-price cost exposure, so pass-through is nil (S2 note 22 cost composition).

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel of Rp697.7bn was 29.9% of the Rp2,333.5bn cost of revenue in FY2025 (S2 note 22); the fleet burns diesel bought chiefly from Pertamina (Rp583.0bn of purchases, S2 note 22), which moves with Brent.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: In FY2025 fuel cost rose 35.5% while the gross margin held at 20.15%, so the per-tonne tariff reset recovered the fuel move across the year (S2). Nine-month 2026 shows the within-year lag: revenue grew 15.1% but gross profit only 2.9%, a 15.5% margin against 20.15%, with deck Brent at US$96 against US$68.1 in FY2025 (S4). The 4.7pp margin fall against an 11.1pp no-pass-through cost rise implies about 58% of the move passed through within nine months; we set 0.58. The remaining 42% is the lagged reset, not a permanent margin loss.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: General and administrative expenses were Rp139.1bn in FY2025, 4.76% of revenue, and Rp123.7bn in nine-month 2026, 5.31% (S2, S4). We hold gross G&A at the 9M2026 run-rate of 5.31% — the line is people and premises, not volume-linked — and net the recurring other operating income that sits below it: FY2025 other operating income of Rp34.8bn comprised a Rp20.7bn MCOL dividend (capitalised in the stake bridge) plus Rp7.3bn asset-sale gains, Rp6.8bn insurance claims and Rp0.1bn other (S2 note 24), so about Rp14.2bn, or 0.46% of revenue, is recurring operating income. That gives a net opex ratio of 4.85%, which keeps the G&A at the observed run-rate while not double-counting the stake dividend.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total depreciation and amortisation was Rp369.2bn in FY2025 (12.6% of revenue, S2 note 30) and Rp315.4bn in nine-month 2026 (13.5%, S4), of which right-of-use fleet amortisation is about half. The data pack carries only Rp8.5bn of D&A, the G&A charge; history is restated from the filings. Held at 13.0%.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total capital expenditure was Rp605.0bn in FY2025 (20.7% of revenue) and Rp498.7bn in FY2024, the segment note's cash capex plus right-of-use fleet additions (S2 note 30); the data pack's cash-capex line alone is Rp109.8bn and understates fleet investment. The nine-month 2026 pause (Rp65.9bn cash capex plus Rp19.7bn of ROU additions) is deployment timing, not evidence the fleet is no longer needed: the leases are three-year terms and Rp287.6bn of minimum lease payments fall due within one year, with a further Rp233.2bn in years two to three (S4 note 11), so the FY2023-24 vintages roll in FY2026-28. We ramp replacement from 5.5% of revenue in FY2026E to 13.5% in FY2028E and 14.5% long run — the 13.0% D&A charge plus about 1.5% for growth in the net asset base. That restores the full replacement charge by FY2028 rather than deferring it to FY2031.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp116.4bn at December 2025, 4.0% of revenue, and Rp113.9bn at December 2024, so the last two year-ends sit at 4.0-4.5% on the data pack's definition (S0). The 30 September 2026 LK shows trade receivables of Rp499.0bn plus inventories of Rp85.0bn against trade payables of Rp234.6bn, about 11-12% of annualised revenue (S4), so the September position is far above the year-end norm. We do not assume a full seasonal reversal: cash paid to suppliers rose 42% on a 15% revenue increase against the prior-year nine months, and payable days fell from about 61 at December 2025 to about 33 at September 2026 (S4), so part of the contraction is structural. We hold 8.0% of revenue, between the year-end history and the September level, and treat the September 11-12% as the downside in the risk section.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22%. The reported 29.9% FY2025 rate is distorted by the non-deductible MCOL mark; excluding the unrealised loss, tax of Rp100.3bn on Rp454.4bn of pre-mark profit is 22.1%, and nine-month 2026 is 21.4% on the same basis (S2, S4). Held at 22%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The fleet leases carry implicit rates of 8.38% to 10.00% (S4 note 11) and the Bank Mandiri investment credit is fixed at 7.5% (S4 note 17); leases are about 90% of the debt stack, so the blended cost is 9.5%. FY2025 finance costs of Rp44.2bn on opening debt of Rp378.6bn were 11.7%, but nine-month 2026 was 8.6% annualised on the larger base (S2, S4).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp15.4bn on an opening cash balance of Rp566.2bn is 2.7% (S2); nine-month 2026 income of Rp14.6bn on opening cash gives 3.4% annualised (S4). Held at 3.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The lease book is amortising: nine-month 2026 lease principal paid was Rp233.0bn against only Rp19.7bn of new right-of-use additions (S4), and total debt fell from Rp612.4bn to Rp532.9bn. The fleet-replacement cycle resumes from FY2028E as the 3-year leases expire, so net repayment fades to zero. The model also carries the Rp43.3bn Bank Mandiri land loan already drawn (S4 note 17).

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Set to zero: the FY2025 non-operating line is the Rp118.5bn unrealised mark-to-market loss on the 2.10% PT Prima Andalan Mandiri stake (S2 note 8), a non-cash item that fluctuates with the share price. The stake itself is valued at market in the bridge, and its dividend income is capitalised there rather than double-counted in the cash flow.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests sit in the subsidiary that holds the port-logistics operations and recorded losses of Rp6.95bn in FY2025 and Rp3.62bn in nine-month 2026 (S2, S4), so the minorities' share of profit is negative. Held at -2.0%, immaterial to equity value.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The board declared Rp196.74bn for FY2025, paid June 2026, on parent net profit of Rp242.53bn — 81% (S4 statement of changes in equity; S2 note 20). The policy is up to 40% of retained earnings after mandatory reserves (S6), and DPS has been Rp12 in each year since listing. Held at 81%, the last actual, not a default cut.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares outstanding were 16,394.97m at December 2025 after treasury shares of 271.03m, which carry a cumulative cost of Rp46.31bn (FY2024 Rp25.52bn plus FY2025 Rp20.79bn, S2 note 18); no further corporate action announced.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House rupiah terminal growth for a domestic coal-logistics service; the deck's long-run Indonesian CPI is 3.28% and the peer median terminal rate is about 3.25%, so we set 3.25% rather than the 4.0% used in the first draft. Coal hauling grows with national output rather than with a commodity rent (S2, S6).

challenges.challenge: The gross-margin forecast rests on a Brent link the last actual contradicts. FY2025 fuel in COGS was Rp697.7bn against Rp514.7bn in FY2024 (+35.5%), while the deck's Brent fell from US$79.8 to US$68.1 (-14.7%) and tonnage was flat (60.31 vs 60.05 Mt): fuel per tonne rose 34.9%. The report states the 35.5% but never reconciles it to Brent, yet sets link2_share 29.9% and link2_pass 50% and uses them to recover the gross margin from 15.3% in FY2026E to 20.1% by FY2030E. That recovery is the main driver of the FY2027 net-profit rebound (Rp225.0bn to Rp321.5bn). If the 2025-26 fuel move is haul-mix or Pertamina pricing rather than Brent, the 50% pass-through and the recovery are unproven.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2025 fuel rose 35.5% while Brent fell 14.7%, but tonnage was flat and revenue per tonne rose 14.4%, so litres per tonne (haul mix) is a real part of the move; the residual is Pertamina's administered diesel price. In 9M2026 fuel rose 46.5% against Brent +41%, which reasserts the link. I re-fit the within-year pass-through from the 9M margin: a 4.7pp fall against an 11.1pp no-pass-through cost rise implies about 58%, so link2_pass is now 0.58 (was 0.50). Added a report paragraph, a fact for FY2024 fuel volume, and FY2024/9M fuel-cost facts. DCF at 0% pass-through Rp170.5, at 50% Rp220.9, at 58% Rp229.0, at 100% Rp271.3; the base-case 12-month value after the liquidity discount is Rp170 at 0% and Rp262 at 100%, so the DCF is above the price at either extreme.

challenges.challenge: The DCF bridge mixes balance-sheet dates. fund record market.debt is Rp558.743bn at 30 Jun 2026 (pack latest_bs) and market.cash is Rp459.150bn at 30 Sep 2026 (restated F42), giving net debt Rp99.594bn. S4 p.5 shows total debt of Rp532.891bn at 30 Sep (lease liabilities Rp478.622bn + Bank Mandiri Rp43.333bn + other financial liabilities Rp10.825bn + consumer Rp0.111bn), so 30 Sep net debt is Rp73.738bn - the Rp73.7bn the report itself quotes in the extreme_call justification. Because market.bs_date is still 2026-06-30, the engine discounts the FY2026E stub from 1 Jul (fraction 0.5038) while the cash balance already includes Q3, double-counting about Rp120bn of Q3 FCFF. On the 30 Sep basis the DCF is Rp252.1, not Rp257.8; on the 30 Jun basis (cash Rp270.9bn) it is Rp246.3.
challenges.answer: Accepted. I took the second route: reverted the cash restatement so the bridge uses the data pack's 30 June cash of Rp270.9bn against its 30 June debt of Rp558.7bn, which makes the cash balance and the discounted H2 2026 stub cover the same period. The Q3 LK still drives the FY2026 forecast but no longer enters the bridge, and the \"restatement.bs_cash\" justification was removed because the restatement is gone. post_bs_review and section 4 now state which balance sheet the bridge uses and why. DCF is Rp229.0 (was Rp257.8); the date-consistency correction is the ~Rp11.5/share you quantify, and the rest of the fall is the other accepted fixes.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is applied to the very denominator the report says cannot be compared. The peer median 17.247x (n=10; BESS 35.3x, SGER 46.5x, TCPI 34.2x, MBSS 29.1x, RMKE 21.6x) is struck on data-pack EBITDA measured before the lease/D&A restatement applied to MAHA, as the report states; applying it to MAHA's restated Rp852.370bn gives Rp907/share (+252% vs the DCF) and lifts v0 from Rp258 to Rp317 and the base target from ~Rp275 to Rp350 (~Rp75, ~20% of the target). The prose says "a multiple in the high teens ... is not a benchmark we would use as a target" and then weights it 10%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The EV/EBITDA weight is set to zero; the blend is DCF 90% and P/BV 10%. The multiple is no longer printed as a method, and section 4 now says explicitly that it is excluded because the peer median is struck on data-pack EBITDA measured before the lease and D&A restatement. multiple_basis and the qc justification were rewritten to match. This is the largest single correction: it removes the ~Rp75 you attribute to the incomparable multiple and takes the target from Rp354 to Rp273 alongside the other fixes.

challenges.challenge: The capex path defers the fleet replacement the lease book implies. Leases are 3-year terms (S4 note 11) and Rp257.066bn of lease liabilities is current (due within 12 months) at 30 Sep 2026 (S4 p.5), against Rp19.735bn of new ROU additions in 9M2026 (F40). The model charges FY2026E capex of 4.5% of revenue (Rp139.4bn) and FY2027E 7.0% (Rp238.5bn), reaching 14.5% only in FY2031; the FY2023-24 ROU vintages mature in FY2026-27. The 9M pause is deployment timing, not evidence the fleet is no longer needed for +6%/+10% revenue growth.
challenges.answer: Accepted. S4 note 11 shows the leases are three-year terms, Rp287.6bn of minimum payments fall due within one year and Rp233.2bn in more than one to three years, so the FY2023-24 vintages do roll in FY2026-28. Replacement now starts from FY2027E: capex is 5.5% of revenue in FY2026E, 11.0% in FY2027E, 13.5% in FY2028E and 14.5% long run. Cumulative FY2026-28 capex is about Rp356bn higher than the first draft, inside your Rp250-400bn estimate, and the DCF is correspondingly lower; the full replacement charge is restored by FY2028 rather than FY2031. Facts F61/F65 carry the maturity profile.

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not reach the two things that carry the value: the terminal assumption and the Bayan book. The bear shocks revenue_growth by -8pp and gross_margin by -2pp on the explicit years only; val.g stays +4.0%, so the terminal value (38.2% of EV) still grows forever. The largest customer, PT Indonesia Pratama/Bayan, was 63.8% of FY2025 revenue (Rp1,863.3bn of Rp2,922.3bn, S2 p.73) and 63.1% of 9M2026; the bear loses only Kideco and Mandiri Intiperkasa (~19%). The report calls concentration "High/High" yet the scenario does not price any Bayan volume loss or a transition-driven terminal decline.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear now runs four shocks: revenue growth -8pp with Indonesia Pratama/Bayan explicitly trimming volumes in the narrative, gross margin -2pp, WACC +2.0pp and terminal growth -3.0pp to 0.25%, i.e. a terminal decline rather than perpetual growth. Base terminal growth is also cut from 4.0% to 3.25%, the deck's long-run CPI, so 39% of EV is no longer assumed to grow at a rate above the deck. The bear value falls to Rp116.6, below the Rp132 price. The deliberate -3.0pp/+2.0pp growth asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications with the energy-transition and deck-CPI evidence.

challenges.challenge: The base case is conservatively below the contract evidence. FY2027E revenue grows +10.0% (Rp3,097.7bn to Rp3,407.4bn, +Rp309.8bn), but the Ade Putra contract alone is ~Rp550bn a year (F38, S8) and starts 6 Oct 2026; if Q4 2026 carries roughly a quarter (~Rp137bn), the FY2027 increment is ~Rp413bn, +13.3% of FY2026E, i.e. the model implies ~Rp100bn of decline in the rest of the book with no source. FY2026E also excludes the Q4 2026 contribution the report's own catalyst says begins then, and is set +6.0% against the 6.4% 9M annualized run-rate.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2026E revenue growth rises from 6.0% to 8.0%, which carries one ramp quarter of the Rp550bn-a-year Ade Putra contract on top of the 9M run-rate. FY2027E rises from 10.0% to 13.3%, a full year of Ade Putra plus the momentum already visible in the 9M customer table (Indonesia Pratama revenue Rp1,470.5bn against Rp1,235.6bn and Kideco Rp220.2bn against Rp184.2bn). That gives FY2026E revenue of Rp3,156.1bn and FY2027E of Rp3,575.9bn, so the model no longer implies an unsourced decline in the rest of the book. Facts F56-F59 carry the customer comparatives.

challenges.challenge: opex_pct is held at 4.8% of revenue against the 9M2026 actual 5.31% (Rp123.7bn on Rp2,331.0bn), which the report itself cites. The model's FY2026E opex is Rp148.7bn, implying Q4 G&A of Rp25.0bn against the 9M quarterly average of Rp41.2bn - a 40% step-down with no source, and inconsistent with the basis that G&A is "people and premises, not volume-linked". Holding 5.31% would add ~Rp15.8bn of cost (~2.2% of FY2026E EBITDA).
challenges.answer: Accepted. Gross G&A is now held at the 9M2026 run-rate of 5.31% of revenue, not 4.8%. Because the model's opex line is net of other operating income, I net the recurring other operating income of about Rp14.2bn (asset-sale gains, insurance claims and other, excluding the MCOL dividend) against it, which gives an opex ratio of 4.85% of revenue. The gross-Q4 step-down you identify is gone; the net change is about Rp1.5bn of cost, with the bulk of the difference supplied by the C8 other-income lines rather than an unsourced cut.

challenges.challenge: The model sets other operating income to zero from FY2026E, but S2 note 24 shows FY2025 other operating income of Rp34.8bn = dividend income Rp20.7bn + gain on sale of fixed assets Rp7.3bn + insurance claims Rp6.8bn + other Rp0.1bn, and 9M2026 already has Rp27.1bn. Only the Rp20.7bn MCOL dividend is legitimately capitalised in the stake bridge; the ~Rp14bn of recurring asset-sale/ insurance income is dropped with no source. This also means part of the -5.7pp calibration gap is definitional, not fuel.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The FY2025 other operating income of Rp34.8bn is split: the Rp20.7bn MCOL dividend is capitalised in the stake bridge, while the Rp7.3bn asset-sale gain, Rp6.8bn insurance claims and Rp0.1bn other, about Rp14.2bn of recurring operating income, are kept in the operating forecast by netting them against gross G&A (see C7).
